headline: High: shared filesystem and broad write/network tools make prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors plausible by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can read/write workspace files and use MCP, so one can place attacker-controlled content where the other may ingest it. Cline’s per-workspace shared state via filesystem and nullclaw’s workspace files plus delegate/MCP surfaces create a plausible default bridge, though no direct parser weakness is evidenced.
conditions: IF either agent reads the other’s workspace files as instructions or tool input
IF a shared MCP server or file bridge is configured between the two agents
mitigations: Separate workspaces and mount points for each agent
Disable shared MCP servers between the agents
Require provenance labels on any cross-agent file handoff
Review and sanitize files before one agent consumes the other’s output

B_data_leakage.rationale: Cline handles model-provider API keys and workspace files, while nullclaw handles API keys, private keys, bearer tokens, and audit logs. Both have broad filesystem access and network egress, so sensitive material can move between them or out to third parties in default workflows; the blast radius includes secrets exfiltration.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace or config directory
IF either agent is allowed to upload file contents or logs to external services
mitigations: Use separate OS users or containers for each agent
Exclude secret-bearing directories from both workspaces
Turn off network egress for one agent during secret handling
Rotate any secrets exposed in shared logs or files
Audit and redact workspace files before cross-agent access

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write the filesystem, modify git state, spawn subprocesses, and use broad network egress. Cline’s shared state is via filesystem, while nullclaw uses durable memory plus workspace files; without explicit locking, concurrent edits to the same repo or config can overwrite each other and corrupt state.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same git repository or workspace directory
IF no external lock or lease mechanism serializes writes
mitigations: Assign disjoint repositories or directories
Enable file or git locking around shared resources
Serialize write-heavy tasks so only one agent mutates state at a time
Use read-only clones for one agent
Check for and resolve conflicts after each write batch

D_cascading_error.rationale: Both agents can act on browser, shell, and file outputs, so one agent’s generated content can become the other’s operational input. Cline’s tool-use loop and nullclaw’s delegate/schedule/spawn surfaces make it easy for unverified outputs to cascade into actions, including commits or external requests, if the orchestrator chains them.
conditions: IF one agent’s output is forwarded to the other without verification
IF the second agent is permitted to execute shell, git, or network actions on that output
mitigations: Insert a human review step between agents
Require schema validation for all cross-agent messages
Disable auto-execution of generated commands
Limit one agent to read-only analysis
Log and diff all downstream actions against the source output

E_compliance.rationale: Nullclaw explicitly touches audit logs, conversation history, memory, and multiple secret classes, while Cline handles model-provider API keys and workspace files. The pair creates a compliance mismatch risk around retention and secret handling, but the profiles do not show a specific residency or certification conflict, so medium is the highest supported severity.
conditions: IF the same regulated data class is stored in both agents’ logs or memory
IF retention or deletion policies differ across the two workspaces
mitigations: Classify data before either agent stores it
Disable or shorten retention for logs and memory
Keep regulated data out of shared workspaces
Document deletion/export procedures for both agents
Review vendor residency and DPA terms before deployment
